tools.name: search
tools.description: Search the corpus. The SOURCE (paper/book) is the unit of every result: each hit lists the findings that made it match (claim, place, period) and why it matched, so you can judge relevance without opening it. Combine free text (`query`) with any filters: `tags` (ALL must be present), `authors`/`places` (any of), `topics` (all), `status`, publication years (`yearFrom`/`yearTo`), deep-time overlap (`from`/`to`, signed years — BCE is negative, so 1200 BCE is -1200) and a lon/lat box. A source matches a period/box/place through its own metadata OR any of its findings. Use the `facets` tool FIRST to discover the tag/author/place/topic vocabulary instead of guessing terms; a filter with an unknown tag returns nothing. Page with `limit`/`offset`; `sort` is relevance|cited|period|year|oldest|title. USE `groupBy` TO SEE **WHEN** AND **WHERE** THE EVIDENCE SITS BEFORE READING SOURCES: groupBy = time | region | time,region | region,time returns a nested tree of counts instead of a list — adaptive time buckets, and/or the gazetteer from continents down — with a few sample sources under each leaf. `depth` (1-3) is how deep it nests, `asOf` (a signed year) is when the region hierarchy is read at (`time,region` reads each bucket at its own midpoint, so the same site moves from Hittite Empire to Phrygia on its own). Counts are NON-ADDITIVE: a source is counted in every bucket its period overlaps and in every place that covers it, so children never sum to their parent — the tree says how many are double-counted. Narrow `from`/`to` or `places` to one bucket and ask again to drill into it. `verbose` (default true): set to false for a compact listing — citekey · title · year · status · period · one why-line, no snippets/matches/summaries. Use when scanning a large result set before drilling in. FTS note: an AND is evaluated within one chunk, so `sea peoples pottery` matches only when all three words appear in the same ~4 000-char section of one source.

tools.name: get_source
tools.description: Fetch one source by citekey. `section` selects what to return: summary (abstract), findings, notes (the agent's article about this source), toc (table of contents: headings with byte offsets into the body), body (the full converted text, sliceable), or all. Default returns summary + findings + notes. `heading` returns only the body chunks under one heading (case-insensitive prefix match). `offset`/`chars` slice the body: chars characters starting at offset (0-based), with a trailing '…N more chars — pass offset=M' when truncated. `fullText: true` is a shorthand for section=body without offset — capped at the configured limit (default 60 000 chars). Bodies are large (mean 450 KB, max 5.7 MB) — to find a word or a quotation inside one source use `passages`; otherwise prefer `search` snippets or a `section`/`heading` slice over the full body. Use after `search` to read what a source says — not to discover sources.

tools.name: passages
tools.description: Find a word, phrase or quotation inside ONE source's full text — `grep` over its body. Returns the passages around each match (the match in **bold**), each with its `offset` into the body (pass it to `get_source` as `offset` to read on) and the heading it sits under, then how many more there are. `query` is matched LITERALLY (no stemming), case-insensitive, accents optional (`Hattusa` finds `Ḫattuša`), curly quotes and dashes as plain ones; its words may span a line break. `regex: true` makes it a Java regex (`^`/`$` per line). `limit` passages (default 10, max 50), `context` characters around each match (default 600, max 3000). Use it to check what a source says about a term instead of paging through `get_source` slices.

tools.name: neighbors
tools.description: Typed edges to/from a source: references, challenges, refutes, updates, superseded_by. The output has two sections: **Sources** (edges where the target resolves to a real source, with its status) and **Topics** (unresolved `references` targets collapsed to a list of article slugs). Use `kinds` to filter by edge kind. An empty result is not evidence of agreement — disagreement edges are extremely sparse in the corpus. Use `contradictions` for a focused disagreement view, not this.

tools.name: graph
tools.description: Source dependency GRAPH: BFS traversal of the citation/relationship network around a source, returning a D3-ready node+link structure. Each node carries citekey, title, year, status and BFS depth. Links carry the edge kind. Use `depth` to control how far to walk (0–4, default 2). Edge kinds include: references, challenges, refutes, updates, superseded_by, supersedes, confirms, cites, foundational_for, compilation_of, review_of, verifies.

citekey.description: Root source citekey to start BFS from

tools.name: contradictions
tools.description: Disagreement edges and contested statuses in the corpus. With a `citekey`: its challenges/refutes/updates/superseded_by edges in both directions, with the other side's year and status. Without: corpus-wide — every source that has such an edge OR whose status is contested|superseded|debunked|retracted. `since` filters on the challenging source's publication year. Edge kinds: references, challenges, refutes, updates, superseded_by. An empty result is not evidence of agreement — disagreement edges are extremely sparse.

citekey.description: Show contradictions for this source only; omit for corpus-wide

since.description: Filter by the challenging source's publication year (signed year, BCE negative)

tools.name: put_source
tools.description: Create or REPLACE an entire source (metadata, summary, body, notes, topics, regions, tags, period, findings, edges) under one citekey. Idempotent, and destructive: anything you omit is erased and every finding is renumbered from #0. Edges are FROM this source, each {dst,kind} (a src naming another source, or a self-edge, is refused). An unknown key is refused, naming it. Use it only to CREATE a source or to deliberately re-import one. To add or correct findings/tags/edges/notes on a source that already exists, use patch_source; never re-upload the whole source.

confidence.description: high | medium | low | contested — another word is refused

strict.description: Refuse the write when its Markdown has a formatting ERROR (a table that will not render, unpaired **, a broken link). Default false: the write goes through and the problems are listed under 'Formatting'.

tools.name: patch_source
tools.description: Selectively enrich an existing source: send ONLY the parts you are changing; everything else is left exactly as it is. Parts: metadata{title,authors,year,venue,doi,status,provenance,calibreId} (null CLEARS year/venue/doi/provenance/calibreId), summary, body, notes (your compiled article about the source), topics, regions, period{start,end} (signed years, BCE negative), tags{add,remove,replace}, findings{add,remove(ids),replace}, edges{add,remove} — edges FROM this source, each {dst,kind}: to record a --refutes--> b, patch a (a src naming another source is refused). Findings keep stable ids '<citekey>#<n>', so one can be removed or re-added individually. Pass ifUpdatedAt with the updatedAt you last read to be told — instead of silently clobbering — when someone else changed the source meanwhile. An unknown or misplaced key (e.g. status outside metadata) is refused, naming it and where it belongs. The answer lists formatting problems in the summary and notes; `strict: true` refuses a patch whose summary or notes have a formatting error. To add or correct findings/tags/edges/notes on a source that already exists, use patch_source; never re-upload the whole source.

strict.description: Refuse the write when its Markdown has a formatting ERROR (a table that will not render, unpaired **, a broken link). Default false: the write goes through and the problems are listed under 'Formatting'.

tools.name: rename_source
tools.description: Give a source a NEW citekey — to correct a misleading one (e.g. a year that is not the publication year: page2024_history for a 1959 book → page1959_history). One transaction: the findings are renumbered '<new>#<n>', every table that stores the citekey follows, and every [[old]] link (labels and anchors kept, short forms like [[beckman2025]] included) is rewritten in article bodies — each rewrite recorded as an article version — and in source notes/summaries. The old citekey stays an alias: every read and every write that names it (put, patch, delete, rename, a reference) goes to the record under its new citekey, and the answer names the new citekey. (get_source, neighbors, graph, export_source, /source/<old> and [[old]] included.) Refused when the new citekey is taken (by a source, or as an old citekey of another source) or is not link-shaped. Use it only to fix an identifier; to change metadata (year, title) use patch_source.

newCitekey.description: The citekey it should have from now on

tools.name: export_source
tools.description: Render a source as the Markdown note it would be on disk: YAML frontmatter (citekey, doi, title, authors, year, venue, status, topics, regions, tags, period_start/period_end, summary, findings) plus the notes body. This is the git-friendly mirror of the database and it round-trips back in through seed. To add or correct findings/tags/edges/notes on a source that already exists, use patch_source; never re-upload the whole source.

tools.name: backup
tools.description: Take a full pg_dump backup of the Histmersion database, server-side, and return the file name, size and SHA-256 checksum. Use it before a bulk reseed, a mass patch, or any other operation you may need to undo. Restoring is NOT available as a tool: it destroys data, and is done by a human with `histmersion restore <file> --force`.

tools.name: config
tools.description: The server's own settings, kept in its settings file (never in the database). `get` shows settings (`key` one, or `prefix` a block such as `acquire`): what the file says, what applies and from where, the default and what the setting does — a credential only as set or not and how it is referred to. `set` (`key`, `value` as a person would type it) and `unset` (`key`) change the file in place, keeping its comments, order, includes and anything written by hand, check the change first (a refused change says why in plain words), keep the old file as .bak and reload the server. A credential is written as a reference — env:NAME or <vault>:<entry> — and `value:` only with `literalConsent`. `reload` reads the file again and switches the running server to it in place; `restart` restarts a server that runs under its service, for the settings only a restart applies (the listening host/port, the bundled runtime, pool sizes). The settings that decide what agents may fetch (acquire.allow-unauthorised, acquire.agents-may-use-unauthorised) are a person's: this tool refuses to change them.

key.description: the setting, e.g. backups.keep (get, set, unset)

value.description: set: the value as a person types it — text, a number, true/false, a list [a, b]

prefix.description: get: the settings under this block, e.g. acquire

literalConsent.description: set: a credential may be written as value:… (the key itself in the file)

tools.name: vacuum
tools.description: Run PostgreSQL VACUUM — with `analyze: true`, VACUUM (ANALYZE), which also refreshes the planner's statistics — over the named `tables`, or over the gazetteer and finding tables a re-seed rewrites (config maintenance.vacuum-tables) when none is named. Use it after `places seed`, a gazetteer load or a place clean-up (`lint --fix` on the place rules), which leave dead row versions behind. It runs as a server job, one table at a time, outside any transaction (no data changes, no table lock beyond VACUUM's own); it answers with the job — follow it with `job_status`.

tools.name: list_articles
tools.description: List/search the compiled articles. `kind` filters to concept|myth|culture|region|timeline|report, `tag` to the articles citing a source with that tag, `title` to a title substring, `query` is full text over the article's title, summary and body (websearch syntax: "phrase", -not, or) plus a title substring. Start here before compiling anything: an article on the topic may already exist, in which case you extend it with patch_article rather than starting a new one. Articles are the COMPILED KNOWLEDGE of this corpus — the concept/myth/culture/region/timeline/report pages a reader reads instead of the papers. Write them by the rules in docs/writing-guide.md: exhaust the filter (every source it returned is used or explicitly excluded), surface disagreements with years, EVERY PARAGRAPH CITES at least one source as [[citekey]] (a paragraph with no citekey is deleted, not rewritten), plain technical language with no filler, specialist terms defined in one clause on first use, and the sections question / what the sources say / disagreements / what is unresolved. Record the article's FILTER (`filter`) and a REASON for each of its sources the body does not cite (`reasons`): the page then generates the Not used list, its counts and the Method note — never write those by hand.

tools.name: check_edits
tools.description: Dry-run a change to an article and see what the review checks would say — nothing is written. `edits` are applied in order to the CURRENT stored body: each is {op: replace|insertAfter|insertBefore|delete, anchor: text copied exactly from the body (it must occur once; whitespace is normalised), text}. tools.name: export_article
tools.description: Render an article as the Markdown note it would be on disk at wiki/<kind>/<slug>.md: YAML frontmatter (type, slug, title, summary, regions, tags, period_start/period_end, and the filter and reasons it is compiled from) plus the body, then the generated Not used and Method sections between markers an import drops. This is the git-friendly mirror of the database and it round-trips back in through seed.

tools.name: article_versions
tools.description: List the edit history of one article (newest first): version id, date, word count and the first 200 chars of the summary at that point. Use it to see how an article changed over time, or to find the version id of a body you want to recover with `article_version`.

tools.name: article_version
tools.description: Fetch the full body of one historical version of an article. Use it to read what the article said before a rewrite, or to recover text that a bad patch overwrote.

tools.name: places
tools.description: The GAZETTEER: places with geometry, alternate/period names and a temporally scoped hierarchy (continent > country > polity > site). Without `id` it SEARCHES by name — use it to turn a name a human wrote ('Anatolia', 'Hatti') into a place **id**, then pass that id as `places` to `search`/`geo_when`: an id matches every finding inside the place's shape AND everything below it in the hierarchy, which a bare name never does. With `id` it SHOWS one place: what it is, when it was valid, what it is part of and what it contains, as an indented tree. `asOf` is a signed year (BCE negative) and selects the hierarchy as it stood then — the same site is under 'Hittite Empire' at -1400 and under 'Phrygia' at -700. Counts are non-additive: a finding on a border belongs to every place that covers it.

query.description: Name or label substring (case-insensitive); `name` is an alias

name.description: Alias of `query` — a place NAME to look up (not full-text search)

id.description: Place id to look up directly

asOf.description: Signed year the gazetteer is read at (omit for all rows)

tools.name: place_names
tools.description: Names ADDED BY HAND to gazetteer places — the names every re-seed keeps (an import replaces a place's other names). Without `name` it LISTS them (of `placeId`, or of every place). With `placeId` and `name` it ADDS that name (`lang`: a language tag such as en, grc, pl; omit when unknown) — use it when a well-known name finds no place in `places` ("Lake Kinneret" for the Sea of Galilee), so the geocoder and `places=` filters know it from then on. With `remove: true` it removes a name added by hand (a name the seed gives cannot be removed). Find the place id with `places` first.

placeId.description: The place (an id from `places`); required with `name`

name.description: The name to add (or remove); omit to list the names added by hand

lang.description: Language tag of the name: en, grc, la, pl …; omit when unknown

remove.description: true: remove this name (only a name added by hand)

tools.name: place_override
tools.description: Curate a gazetteer place by hand, over what its source says — KIND (site | region | polity | people | feature) and/or PERIOD (`periodStart`/`periodEnd`, signed years, BCE negative; one side alone leaves the other open) and/or POINT (`pointLat`/`pointLon`, for a place known by a point whose stored point is wrong; `reason` must name the gazetteer value it comes from — a Pleiades representative point, a Wikidata coordinate — never an estimate). Every re-seed and re-import keeps it, and the place's findings are matched again at once (a site takes findings within the point tolerance; a region, polity or people known only by a point takes only the findings that name it). Use it when a source files a place wrongly — Pleiades' Regio XII of Rome as an urban site, one of 14 regiones. `reason` says what evidence the decision rests on. With `placeId` alone, or nothing, it LISTS the overrides (with what the source says); `reset: true` drops one and restores the source's kind, period and point. `mergeInto` (a place id) merges the place into the one it is the same as (findings, links and references move; its id resolves there) — for a duplicate a source withdrew; `remove: true` deletes a place nothing refers to. Neither comes back with a re-seed. Find the place id with `places` first.

placeId.description: The place (an id from `places`); required to set or reset

kind.description: The kind it is: one of region, polity, site, feature, people

reason.description: Why: the evidence the decision rests on (with a point: the gazetteer value it comes from)

reset.description: true: drop the override and restore what the source says

mergeInto.description: The id of the place this one is the same as: merge it there

remove.description: true: delete this place (only when nothing refers to it)

pointLat.description: Latitude of the corrected point (with pointLon) — a place known by a point only

pointLon.description: Longitude of the corrected point (with pointLat)

tools.name: add_place
tools.description: Add a POINT place to the gazetteer that it does not have — only after `places` found nothing under any of its names (otherwise give the existing place a name with `place_names`). `source` is required and must say where the coordinates come from (a gazetteer or Wikidata id, a map, a publication): never estimate a point. `kind`: site | region | feature | polity; `names` are further names; `periodStart`/`periodEnd` are signed years (BCE negative) when the place existed only then. The place is this collection's own (`local_<label>` unless `id` is given), carried in a bundle and never touched by a re-seed. Refused when the id is taken.

kind.description: one of region, polity, site, feature, people

source.description: where the coordinates come from (a gazetteer id, a map, a publication)

tools.name: periods
tools.description: NAMED PERIODS: PeriodO definitions of historical/archaeological periods (Bronze Age, Late Minoan IB, Old Babylonian, Yamnaya…), each with its span in signed years (BCE negative), its region and the published authority that states the range. Without `id` it SEARCHES by label (`query`), exact `region`, and/or overlap with `from`..`to`; with `id` it SHOWS one period with what it is part of and how it is divided. Use it to turn a period name in a question into the years to pass as `from`/`to` to `search`/`geo_when` — and cite the authority, since two authorities date the same name differently.

id.description: Period id (a PeriodO id such as p0ds9qjq7b2) to show

from.description: Signed year (BCE negative): periods overlapping from..to

to.description: Signed year (BCE negative): periods overlapping from..to

tools.name: events
tools.description: EVENTS database: CIDOC-CRM compatible historical events with four-point time-spans, compositional hierarchy (parent_id), causal/temporal edges (Allen interval algebra) and participant roles. Without `id` it LISTS events; with `id` it SHOWS one event including its datings, edges, participants and scale (local|regional, stated or derived). Use `kind` to filter (a kind — eruption, earthquake, battle, siege, war, migration… — or a group: natural | human) and `historicity` (attested|inferred|contested|legendary|mythic). An event's TIER is `attested` (a source in the corpus attests it) or `catalogue` (known only from a catalogue — a research lead, not evidence); `show` lists the catalogues with licence and citation, the attesting sources, the findings near it and the sources that may discuss it (see `event_links`).

query.description: Text search over event label and description

id.description: Event id to look up directly (omit for listing)

kind.description: Filter: a kind (eruption|earthquake|tsunami|flood|drought|climate_event|epidemic|famine|battle|naval_battle|siege|war|revolt|treaty|polity_formation|collapse|destruction|migration|invasion|technological_change|cultural_shift|era|…) or natural | human

from.description: Overlap: events whose outer span reaches at or after this signed year

to.description: Overlap: events whose outer span reaches at or before this signed year

title.description: Case-insensitive substring of the event's label

tools.name: patch_event
tools.description: Update fields of one EVENT without replacing it: label, kind, historicity, description, citekey (its primary source), parentId (the event it is part of), placeId (a gazetteer place id — where it happened), its own geometry (GeoJSON `geometry`, or a point as `lat`/`lon`), and `scale`: local (a battle — one place) | regional (an era, a migration — across a region) | auto (forget the stated scale; it is derived from the kind, then the place's kind). The map's playback draws a local event as a point and label at its site, a regional one as a label at the region's centre with its outline. `wikidata`: the Wikidata item the event is (Q…; "" clears it) — where `histmersion media import` reads its picture. On an event a CATALOGUE import created (GVP, NOAA, Wikidata) every changed field (label, kind, timeSpan, historicity, description, geometry) is recorded as a correction and KEPT across re-imports of that catalogue (retired once the catalogue agrees, flagged as a conflict when it changes to something else — `event_corrections`). Returns the event as `events` with `id` shows it.

scale.description: local | regional | auto (clear: derived from kind, then place kind)

placeId.description: Gazetteer place id where the event happened (see `places`)

geometry.description: The event's own geometry as GeoJSON (Point or Polygon)

lat.description: The event's own point, latitude (with lon; instead of geometry)

lon.description: The event's own point, longitude (with lat)

wikidata.description: The Wikidata item the event is (Q…); "" clears it

tools.name: attestations
tools.description: ATTESTATIONS: granular source references linking entities (findings, events, places, edges) to specific passages in a source. W3C Web Annotation selectors: TextQuoteSelector (quote/prefix/suffix), TextPositionSelector (charStart/charEnd), chunk ordinals, page labels, IIIF canvas+xywh, CTS URNs. Without `id` it LISTS attestations filtered by citekey/targetType/targetId; with `id` it SHOWS one attestation.

id.description: Attestation id to look up directly (omit for listing)

tools.name: put_attestation
tools.description: Create a new attestation linking an entity to a specific passage in a source. Returns the created attestation with its generated id. Target types: finding|event|event_dating|place|edge.

prefix.description: TextQuoteSelector: text immediately before the quote

suffix.description: TextQuoteSelector: text immediately after the quote

charStart.description: TextPositionSelector: character offset start in OCR body

charEnd.description: TextPositionSelector: character offset end in OCR body

tools.description: Delete an attestation by its id.

tools.name: goals
tools.description: Research GOALS: the project's research programs and topics. Without `slug` it LISTS goals filtered by status (planned|seeding|compiled|reviewed|done); with `slug` it SHOWS one goal with its sub-goals, links (sources, articles, queries, queue items), schedules and approved plan.

slug.description: Goal slug to look up directly (omit for listing)

tools.name: put_goal
tools.description: Create or replace a research goal. A goal tracks a research program: slug (kebab-case id), title, status (planned|seeding|compiled|reviewed|done), notes (progress), tags, regions, period.

periodStart.description: Signed year the goal's period begins (BCE negative); alone = from then on

periodEnd.description: Signed year the goal's period ends (BCE negative); alone = until then

tools.description: Update specific fields of a goal without replacing the whole row.

periodStart.description: New start of the period (signed year, BCE negative); given alone, the end stays as stored

periodEnd.description: New end of the period (signed year, BCE negative); given alone, the start stays as stored

budgetUsd.description: Cost cap (USD) of the agent runs started for this goal; 0 clears it

tools.name: agent_state
tools.description: Agent STATE: key-value JSONB store that survives across sessions. Without `key` it LISTS all keys; with `key` it SHOWS one entry; with `key` + `value` it SETS (upserts).

key.description: State key to get or set (omit for listing all keys)

value.description: JSON string value to set (omit to just read the key)

tools.name: delete_agent_state
tools.description: Delete an agent state key.

tools.name: ingest
tools.description: OCR a PDF/EPUB into a source and keep its figures. Give EITHER `path` (a path the SERVER can see) OR `base64` (the document itself, for smaller files) plus a `citekey`. This returns immediately with a job id, because converting a long scan takes minutes: poll `job_status` until it is done|failed. `quality` runs the slow, accurate OCR path (use it for image-only scans); `force` accepts a file already stored under another citekey. When the citekey already exists only its body and figures are replaced — findings, tags and notes are left alone — so re-OCR never costs enrichment. Optional title/authors/year/doi are used ONLY when the source is being created. `acquireItem` names the acquisition-queue item this document fulfils: the job ticks it off (`ingested as [[citekey]]`) when it succeeds, and leaves it open when it fails. Without it, the job ticks off every open acquisition item that names the source's DOI, and lists items with a similar title in its progress as possible matches — those are never closed for you.

citekey.description: Citekey to store the source under

quality.description: Use the slow, accurate OCR path (docling)

force.description: Accept a file already stored under another citekey

acquireItem.description: Id of the acquisition-queue item this document fulfils; ticked off when the OCR job succeeds

tools.name: job_status
tools.description: Where an OCR job got to: queued|running|done|failed, with its progress line or the reason it failed. Give `id` for one job, or omit it to list the recent ones — filtered on the server by `status`, `kind` (ingest, reocr, agent, media-import, …), `since` / `until` (2026-10-01, an ISO instant, or 7d / 12h ago) and `subject` (text in what it is about); the listing heads with the counts per kind. A job that says 'interrupted' was killed by a server restart — re-run the same ingest, it is idempotent.

id.description: Job id to check (omit for a listing)

before.description: Listing: the next older page — the id of the last job shown

kind.description: Filter listing: these job kinds (ingest, reocr, agent, media-import, events-import, init, …)

since.description: Filter listing: started at or after 2026-10-01, an ISO instant, or 7d / 12h / 30m ago

until.description: Filter listing: started before the end of 2026-10-01, or an ISO instant

subject.description: Filter listing: text in what the job is about (citekey, target, detail) or the start of its id

tools.name: job_control
tools.description: Pause, resume or cancel a job by `id` (`action`: pause | resume | cancel). A long background job — a picture or event import, a base-map download, an acquisition re-check, the init job's gazetteer loads — stops after the part it is on: paused it keeps what it did and, resumed, goes on with the parts it had not done; cancelled it is recorded as cancelled. An agent run takes its own pause, resume and cancel. Other jobs (an OCR, a vacuum) run as one piece and are refused. Only when the user asked for it.

tools.name: activity
tools.description: Research › Activity: agent runs, background jobs, worklog lines and the person's own decisions in ONE list, newest first, each naming what it touched (goal, run or job, source, article, list item, approval). `show`: all (default) | running | agents | jobs | yours | problems; `since` (2026-10-01, an ISO instant, or 7d / 12h ago); `goal` = one research goal's history; `limit` (default 30, at most 200); `before` = the cursor the last page gave, for the next older one. Use to see what happened recently or what is going on now.

tools.name: log
tools.description: The structured log: what happened, step by step — answered requests, MCP tool calls, provider calls, problems and every database write statement — each with the trace that links the steps of one request or job. Filters: `trace` (an answer's Histmersion-Trace), `job`, `run` (an agent run's id), `source` (citekey), `problem` (an id an answer named; alone: every step of the trace it was raised in), `label` (a client's Histmersion-Trace-Label), `kind` (one of RequestAnswered, RequestsCounted, ProviderCalled, Written, ProblemRaised, Lost, ToolCalled, WritesCounted), `since` / `until` (a date, an ISO instant, or 7d / 12h / 30m ago), `limit` (default 100, at most 1000), `before` (the cursor for the next older page), `from` (database, the default, falling back to the file; or file). Use to answer "what happened to job X / source Y / request Z".

tools.name: assets
tools.description: The figures stored with a source — name, mime, pixel size and the URL each is served at. The Markdown body links them as `assets/<name>`; `get_source` rewrites those to absolute URLs you can fetch. Use to check what figures are available — not to read the source.

tools.name: patch_asset
tools.description: Update metadata on an asset — kind (figure/photo/map/plan/scan), caption, license, geom (lat/lon) and period (periodStart/periodEnd as signed years).

kind.description: Asset kind: figure, photo, map, plan, scan

tools.name: asset_links
tools.description: Search/show ASSET LINKS — semantic relationships between assets and entities. Filter by citekey, asset name, target_type (event/finding/place/source/article), target_id. With `create` fields, creates a new link instead.

citekey.description: Filter by citekey (or required for create)

asset.description: Filter by asset name (or required for create)

targetType.description: Filter by target type: event, finding, place, source, article

relation.description: Set to create a link: depicts, taken_at, illustrates, page_of

tools.name: delete_asset_link
tools.description: Delete an asset link by id.

tools.name: merge_plan
tools.description: Plan the import of another Histmersion collection's bundle into this one (read-only: it decides nothing and writes nothing). Lists EVERY issue in one run — two citekeys for one work, one citekey for two works, differing DOIs/years/statuses, records changed on both sides, articles that diverged — each with a stable id (`S-3c1e7a2b`), the evidence, and the decisions it allows (left = this collection, right = the bundle). `bundle` is the sha256 of a bundle uploaded to the server (the user runs `histmersion merge plan <file>`, which uploads it and prints the sha256). `resolve` maps issue ids to decisions (`keep-left`, `keep-right`, `both`, `map:<citekey>`, …) to see what would remain; `editions` is merge|separate. Present the plan to the user; scholarly decisions (statuses, editions, articles) are theirs — never resolve them on their behalf.

bundle.description: sha256 of a bundle uploaded to the server (`histmersion merge plan <file>` prints it)

editions.description: merge | separate: answers every year-gap (edition) question at once

all.description: List every default, info line and match, not only the first few

tools.name: merges
tools.description: What this collection took in from other Histmersion collections (read-only). `action`: `list` (default) — the merges, newest first, with the bundle, where it came from, the plan and the backup taken; `show` with `id` (a merge id or its first characters) — one merge's report (sources merged, new, renamed, articles merged three-way…), its resolutions and the decisions it remembers; `ledger` — the merge ledger of one record (`uid`: a uid, here or merged away, or a citekey) or of one merge (`id`): which record of the other collection each one here came from, and the redirects of merged-away uids. Applying a merge is the user's (`histmersion merge apply`, or the /merge screen) — never an agent's.

id.description: A merge id, or its first characters (show; ledger of one merge)

uid.description: ledger: the record — a uid (here, or merged away) or a citekey

tools.name: rename_label
tools.description: Give an article a new slug, an event a new id, a goal a new slug, or a gazetteer place a new id (`kind`: article | event | goal | place). One transaction: what points at it follows (an article's versions, links and every [[old]] in other articles — each rewrite recorded as a version; an event's attestations and asset links; a goal's sub-goals, links and schedules; a place's names, parents, footprints, events, attestations and finding assignments). The old one stays an alias: every read and every write that names it (put, patch, delete, rename, a reference) goes to the record under its new one, and the answer names the new one. (get_article / events / goals / places show the record under its new one, a places filter on the old id still matches.) Refused when the new label is taken or is an old label of another record. For a source's citekey use rename_source.

from.description: The current slug (article, goal) or id (event, place)

to.description: The new one: lower-case letters, digits, '_', '.' and '-'

tools.name: lint
tools.description: Health-check the corpus and get a Markdown report grouped by rule. 34 rules: dangling-edges, unresolved-short-citekeys, no-findings, no-period, no-regions, empty-summary, unassessed-status, duplicate-doi, duplicate-sha256, orphan-sources, stale-chunks, undated-findings, unlocated-findings, legacy-figure-links, dangling-article-links, non-canonical-tag, missing-year, year-citekey-mismatch, author-pipe, article-filler, article-uncited-paragraph, article-thin-summary, article-critique-pairing, superseded-without-edge, article-markdown, note-markdown, finding-geocode, finding-unplaced, place-kind, place-grid-point, place-imported-point-area, finding-placeholder, media-licence, event-correction-conflict. Run it after a batch of ingestion to find dead reference targets, un-enriched sources (no findings / period / regions / summary), sources still at status=unassessed, duplicate DOIs, non-canonical tags, year/citekey mismatches, article filler phrases, uncited paragraphs, findings that carry neither a date nor a place, and Markdown that will not display as written (article-markdown, note-markdown). Pass `rules` to run a subset, or `fix: true` to first apply the two safe repairs — unify unambiguous short citekey targets and rebuild missing full-text chunks (with `rules: ["finding-geocode"]`, also move the findings an older geocoder misplaced; with `rules: ["finding-unplaced"]`, give a point to the findings whose place name the gazetteer now knows; with `rules: ["place-kind"]`, reclassify the point-only regions that are peoples, provinces or settlements and merge withdrawn duplicates; with `rules: ["place-grid-point"]`, move atlas-grid-square points to their linked record's point; with `rules: ["place-imported-point-area"]`, remove the GeoNames/Wikidata regions and polities known only by a point — bounded per call: call again while `fixed` says some are still to remove) — and report the state afterwards. Pass `article` (a slug), `source` (a citekey) or `text` (Markdown not stored yet) instead to check just that one for FORMATTING problems, each with line, column, excerpt and what goes wrong; with `fix: true` the wording-safe repairs are applied to it (for `text`, the repaired text is returned). Use after ingestion, after writing an article, or to diagnose data integrity — not for searching.

rules.description: Run only these rules (omit for all); an unknown rule is a 400

fix.description: First apply safe repairs (resolve short edge targets, reindex stale chunks), then report; with article/source/text, apply the wording-safe formatting repairs to it

article.description: Check one article's body and summary for formatting problems (a slug)

source.description: Check one source's summary and notes for formatting problems (a citekey)

text.description: Check Markdown that is not stored yet (e.g. an article body before put_article)

field.description: What `text` is: body (an article body, the default), summary or notes

tools.name: queue
tools.description: The project's bookkeeping, as three lists: `acquire` (what the USER must buy/borrow/download), `tasks` (the agent's backlog) and `log` (the dated worklog). One tool, one `action`: `list` shows the open items of `list` with their ids (`all: true` also shows done items and the file's prose blocks), `add` appends `text` under an optional `topic`, `done` closes item `id`, `recheck` runs the acquisition list's legal re-check now (closes the items the corpus holds with their text, tries a few due ones through the legal open-access chain only; `id` = that item alone, `limit` = at most that many tried, `all: true` = every open item with a DOI, due or not, past the daily caps; `dryRun: true` only lists what it would close and try; a pass of more than one item runs as a job — follow it with job_status). This is where a queue/tracker/changelog belongs — never write one as a new file. `topic` groups items under a heading; on `log` it defaults to today's date, so an added line lands in today's entry. `add` requires `createdBy`, who adds the item: `plugin` and `workflow` (both), and the agent as `agentDefinition`, `provider` and `model` (all three, or none for a step without a model).

action.description: What to do: list | add | done | recheck (the acquisition list's legal re-check)

topic.description: Group the item under this heading (defaults to today's date for log)

reason.description: Why this item is on the list / what research direction it serves (for action=add)

id.description: The item id (for action=done; for action=recheck: that acquisition item only)

all.description: Include done items and prose blocks (for action=list); for action=recheck: every open acquisition item with a DOI, due or not, past the caps (a job)

dryRun.description: action=recheck: list what it would close and try; no fetcher is asked, nothing stored

limit.description: action=recheck: try at most this many due items (default acquire.recheck.per-pass)

tools.name: query
tools.description: Run ONE read-only SQL statement against the Histmersion Postgres/PostGIS store and get columns + rows back as a Markdown table. Use it for the questions `search`/`facets`/`histogram` cannot express — cross-tabulations, counts by two dimensions, set differences. The statement runs in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement timeout and a row cap, so INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/CREATE/DROP are refused by Postgres itself; SELECT only. Deep time is an int8range of SIGNED years (BCE negative) — read the inclusive upper bound as `upper(period) - 1`. Geometry is PostGIS; use ST_X/ST_Y/ST_AsText. Tables: (schema unavailable — call the schema endpoint).

sql.description: One read-only SQL statement (Postgres refuses writes)

tools.name: schema
tools.description: List the tables, columns and types that `query` can read (from the live information_schema). Use to check column names before writing SQL — not for searching the corpus.

tools.name: backups
tools.description: List the backup archives on the server (pg_dump -Fc), newest first: filename, size and timestamp. Read-only — use it to check whether a backup exists before a bulk operation. Creating a backup is the `backup` tool; restoring is `histmersion restore` (human only).

tools.name: bookmarks
tools.description: READ ONLY: the person's own bookmarks, newest first — the sources, articles, events, places, pictures and goals they marked, places on the map, saved views of Explore (filters, map position, span) and periods. `kind` narrows to one (source | article | event | place | picture | goal | view | point | period); `query` = words the bookmark's name or the item's title holds; `limit` (default 200). Use to learn what the person cares about. You cannot add, change or remove a bookmark: only the person does, in the web UI or the CLI.

tools.name: notes
tools.description: READ ONLY: the person's own notes (Markdown), last changed first, each with what it was left on — a source, article, event, place, picture, goal, or a point on the map. `id` = one note in full; `kind` and `item` (a citekey, slug or id) = the notes left on one item; `query` = words in the note or the item's title; `limit` (default 200). Read them as the person's own thoughts, not as sources: never cite a note as evidence. You cannot add, change or remove a note: only the person does, in the web UI or the CLI.

tools.name: event_links
tools.description: Link EVENTS to the corpus without guessing. With `id`: the sources that MAY discuss the event — their findings near it in time and space, passages of their text naming it (label, other names, aliases in other languages) — each scored, PROPOSED and unconfirmed. `confirm` writes an attestation (quote + character offsets) for a source ONLY from a passage that names the event; `reject` stops proposing one. Without `id`: LEADS — catalogue events (eruptions, earthquakes, battles… from the Smithsonian GVP, NOAA NCEI, Wikidata) that no source in the corpus discusses, with the corpus's findings around them counted and the commands to search the literature. A catalogue event is a research lead, never evidence: do not cite it in prose.

id.description: The event; omit to list LEADS (catalogue events no source discusses)

recompute.description: Recompute the event's proposed sources first

confirm.description: Citekeys to confirm: each becomes an attestation from a passage of its text naming the event (refused when none does)

from.description: Leads: events overlapping from this signed year

to.description: Leads: events overlapping up to this signed year

kind.description: Leads: a kind (eruption, battle…) or natural | human

tools.name: event_corrections
tools.description: The fields of CATALOGUE events (GVP, NOAA, Wikidata imports) a person corrected by hand with `patch_event`: each keeps the person's value over the catalogue's on every re-import. A correction is retired automatically (`agreed`) once the catalogue says the same; when the catalogue changes the field to something else it stays applied and is flagged `conflict` for review (conflicts are listed first). Each line: the field, the person's value, what the catalogue said then and, in conflict, what it says now.

tools.name: start_run
tools.description: Start an embedded agent pipeline on the SERVER (off unless the server has agents enabled). Pipelines: `enrich-source` <source> — read one source and propose its summary, classification, period, findings (each with a verbatim quote) and notes; code verifies and patches; `review-article` <article> — the adversarial review panel on one article (rules reviewer, cold reader, skeptic in parallel), merged by code into the article's review ledger, the skeptic ruling on each open pair of its critique checklist; with fix, a fixer revises it (code adds the citations a paragraph already names and guards closed findings), each reviewer verifies the findings it claims fixed and the edited passages, until no major finding remains — then a full panel confirms, deferring what it finds new to the next run; `plan-goal` <goal> — propose sub-goals, search queries and candidate works (DOIs checked upstream by code) for one goal; nothing is created until a person approves the plan; `compile-article` <article> — compile a new article, or a section to append to an existing one, from the sources a filter returns: verified claim table, evidence model, draft, code self-check, then a person approves before anything is written, and a review-article run with fix follows; `currency-check` <goal> — assess and followups over a goal's sources (no model): retractions applied as assess does, disagreement edges to sources in the corpus proposed for approval, citing papers outside it queued for acquisition; `acquisition-sweep` <goal> — discover new works for a goal's queries, a model ranks them against the goal, and the relevant ones become acquisition items — never one already in the corpus or the queue; a watcher that opted in ingests the legal open-access ones (capped per day, legal open access only); `infer-filter` <article> — propose the coverage filter (query, topics, tags) of an article that records none; code runs it against the corpus and the article's own citations, and a person approves it (agents.approvals.article-filter) before it is recorded; `hint-effect` <manager> — read one hint a person gave a process manager and propose the structured action it asks for (hold, prioritise or skip items, or a settings change); code checks the action names real items and settings, and it is applied only when a person approves it; `propose-articles` <goal> — propose the articles a research area should have, each with a slug, title and filter; code checks every slug is free, every filter returns enough sources and none overlaps an article of the area by half, and a person ALWAYS approves the plan before the seeding manager compiles them. Returns the run id at once; the run is checkpointed, budgeted and resumable. Check it with `run_status`. Use instead of doing the same steps yourself when the server's agents are on.

tools.name: list_approvals
tools.description: Changes embedded agent runs PROPOSED and a person decides: a source's status, or a disagreement edge (challenges, refutes, updates, superseded_by), each with the evidence and the verified quote it rests on; a goal's plan (sub-goals, queries, works) or an article a run compiled, which the run WAITS for. Default: the open ones; `state` = open, approved, rejected, failed or all; `kind` = any of status-change, edge, goal-plan, article-publish, article-filter, article-plan, hint-effect; `subject` = text in what it is about (a slug, a manager, a citekey); `goal` = one goal's; `decidedBy` = person, autopilot or auto. The listing heads with the counts per kind and per decider. `digest: true` = the digest instead: everything waiting for a person by kind (how many, the oldest, who decides them now, the subjects, the ids) and the manager items held for a person.

tools.name: decide_approval
tools.description: Approve or reject one open approval by `id`. Approving APPLIES the change through the ordinary source patch (status or edge), or lets the waiting run apply its plan or write its article; rejecting keeps it on record. Without `id`, a whole group at once: every open approval of `kind`, about `subject`, or in `ids` (they narrow together), the oldest first, at most `limit`; `dryRun: true` lists what it would decide. Decide only what the user asked you to, or what you have verified against the record yourself.

id.description: The approval's id (from list_approvals); without it, a group at once (kind, subject, ids)

tools.description: A research goal's schedules — the sweeps of its watcher manager `watch:<goal>` (created PAUSED: a person resumes it with the `manager` tool or the Managers window; it runs only while the server's agents are enabled): `currency` (assess + followups over the goal's sources; disagreement edges proposed for approval) and `acquisition` (search the goal's queries; a model picks what to add to the acquisition list). With `cron` (five fields in UTC, or @daily/@weekly/@monthly; the watcher's one cron, shared by both) sets one; `remove: true` takes it out of the watcher; with neither, lists every schedule. The daily/monthly cost caps are checked before each start.

goal.description: The goal's slug (omit with kind to list every schedule)

tools.name: agent_models
tools.description: The server's embedded-agent models: each step role's CHAIN (models tried in order; the first with allowance left is used), and each allowance (tokens/USD per rolling window, a reserve) with what was used, what is left and when a window frees. `quota: true` instead shows the subscription pools (Claude plan, ChatGPT plan): each window's use against its floor, its reset, how old the reading is, the hold switch. `doctor: true` checks every provider without spending anything (keys, the free model listing, prices, the claude/codex/opencode CLIs and their logins).

tools.description: Change the embedded agents' models (saved in the database over the server's config): with `role` and `models`, that role's chain (provider:model, first choice first, e.g. claude-code:sonnet, anthropic:<model>, local:<model>); with `target` (provider:model, or provider:* for every model of a provider) and `limits` (e.g. "2M tokens/5h", "5 usd/day") plus `reservePct`, that allowance. `reset: true` drops the saved value (config applies again). With `pool` (claude-plan, chatgpt-plan): `hold` true/false pauses or releases all agent use of that subscription, `floors` ("five_hour=30, seven_day=25"; "" = config's) the share of each window that must stay left; `refresh: true` takes a fresh reading now (without `pool`: every pool; the Claude plan's costs one minimal model turn). tools.name: manager
tools.description: The server's persistent process managers (docs/research-process-managers.md): each drives work items to an end — the `review` manager runs `review-article` with fix on one article after another until no MAJOR is left, and stops an article with a task when more runs would not help (omission churn, no progress, a finding reopened or escalated, too many runs; an article with no coverage filter gets one inferred first); `enrich` enriches sources (what an ingest feeds); `seed:<goal>` proposes a research area's articles (a person approves the plan) and compiles them; `watch:<goal>` runs a research area's acquisition sweep and currency check on its cron (weekly by default; ingesting legal open-access finds only when a person opted it in). `action`: `list` (every manager), `show` (one: items in flight, hints, events), `create` (`kind` review|enrich|seed|watch, `goal` for seed and watch, `cron` optional; created paused), `pause` (no new runs; `runs: true` pauses its runs too), `resume`, `enqueue` (`kind` review|extend|enrich|seed and `target`: an article, a citekey/article/goal to enrich, a goal to seed — routed to the right manager, put first), `hold` (`target` until `until` a date or `untilSource` a DOI or citekey exists), `hint` (`text`: a note its runs' fixer and skeptic read; `item` scopes it to one target, `once` to the next run; `effect` = a structured action you PROPOSE — hold/prioritise/skip targets or `config` settings — recorded as a hint-effect approval and applied only when a person approves it; `suggest: true` asks the server's model to propose one), `autopilot` (no `on`: the status — per research goal its stage, managers, sources, articles, open approvals, last activity and pace, and the watchers' ingest backlog; `on: true|false` turns the autopilot on — every goal gets its seeding manager and watcher and moves from planned to reviewed by itself — or off), `drain` (nothing new starts while the runs in flight finish — the autopilot's status says DRAINED once none is queued or running, safe for a deploy; `on: false` lifts it), `mode` (the two as one choice, as the web UI shows it: `mode: working` — on, nothing held back; `finish` — finish current work, then pause (the drain); `pause` — pause now (the autopilot off)), `repair-acquire` (the acquisition items a watcher's sweep created for legal open-access works move into the watchers' ingest backlog, to be ingested within the daily caps; a person's items are never touched; `dryRun: true` lists what it would do), `focus` (the autopilot's focus: at most max-active-goals goals are active for model work, chosen finish-first — articles to review, then to compile, then enough sources, depth-first within a tree, then a person's priority, then the oldest; the others' model-using items are held, ingestion is not. No `focus`: the active goals with why and what each waits for, the queue, the goals that cannot use a slot; `focus: pin|unpin` with `goal`, `focus: priority` with `goal` and `value`, `focus: max` with `value` (0 = no cap; no value: back to the config)). Change only what the user asked for.

tools.name: scheduler
tools.description: The server's central agent scheduler: ONE decision per managers' tick admits the managers' pending work across every job type (goal plans, article proposals, candidate sweeps and their ranking, currency checks, enrichment, compiles, extensions, coverage filters, reviews) within the AI allowance — the runs at once, each plan pool's calls in flight, the budgets and daily caps; a run waiting for a person's approval holds no place. Priorities: the goal's (the focus's pins and priorities), the job type's, plus aging; an item that waited max-wait-hours goes next, every job type gets a minimum share, goals still gathering sources keep a place. `action`: `status` (default: the strategy, resources, the last pass's starts and the queue with why each item waits and what it waits behind; `limit` = waiting items shown), `queue` (only the waiting items, in order), `why` (`item`: one manager item's id or the target of an open item — why it is where it is), `strategy` (`strategy`: type-balanced | goal-first | default — switches it live; change it only when the user asked), `stalls` (the unfinished goals with no progress in `days` days, each with the reason it stands still and the command that unblocks it).

limit.description: status, queue: how many waiting items to show (default 50; queue 200)

tools.name: discover
tools.description: Find LITERATURE THAT IS NOT IN THE CORPUS YET — the trailhead into a new topic. Three modes, pick one: `query` searches OpenAlex by relevance (or `sort: cited` for the most-cited work in the field; start a topic with `<topic> review`, `since` and `sort: cited` for recent reviews); `doi` fetches normalised metadata for one paper; `wikipediaUrl` harvests every DOI a Wikipedia article cites — SUPPLEMENTARY only, to catch a gap after the database searches and the citation graph (`refs`, `followups`), never the starting point or the main channel. Each result carries the citekey it WOULD get and whether the corpus already has it, so `notInDb: true` gives you exactly the delta to ingest. Use the `search` tool instead when you want what we already hold; this one goes out to the internet.

tools.name: refs
tools.description: The reference list a paper DEPOSITED with Crossref, with each entry resolved to a stored source where we have it. Use it to see what a paper builds on, and with `apply: true` to record those as `references` edges so `neighbors` can walk them. Input is a citekey or a DOI.

tools.name: assess
tools.description: Is this paper safe to rely on? Checks the local Retraction Watch mirror, Crossref's retraction/correction/expression-of-concern notices and the citation metrics, and returns a verdict: retracted | corrected | current | low-impact | unassessed. ALWAYS run this before citing a source you have not checked, and with `apply: true` to write the verdict into the source's `status` (a retraction becomes status=retracted). `apply` only overwrites an `unassessed` status — one already set (contested, foundational, …) is kept and reported — unless `forceStatus: true`; a retraction is always written. Input is a citekey or a DOI. `updateRetractions: true` instead starts a refresh of the whole Retraction Watch mirror (it runs in the background — call again to see whether it has finished); do that periodically, not per paper.

tools.name: followups
tools.description: What came AFTER this paper — the citation graph forward. Returns the papers citing it with Semantic Scholar's citation intents, the influential-citation flag and the actual citation contexts, plus a proposed edge kind for each (confirms | challenges | refutes | supersedes | cites) read from those contexts. This is how you answer "is this still accepted?" and "has it been debunked?". `apply: true` records the proposed edges for the citing papers that are already in the corpus. `since` limits to papers published from that year on.

tools.name: ingest_doi
tools.description: Bring a paper INTO the corpus from its identifier: metadata from OpenAlex, then a LEGAL open-access PDF (Unpaywall → CORE → OpenAlex OA locations → Europe PMC/PMC → arXiv → repository landing pages resolved one step (Zenodo, an institutional repository's citation_pdf_url); else PMC's JATS full text), then the ingest job, then its reference edges, then an assessment. Idempotent: re-ingesting an existing citekey updates its metadata and never wipes enrichment; one with no original yet (metadata only) is fetched and converted, one that has its original keeps it unless `refetch: true`. When no open-access copy exists the source is still created from metadata and the report tells you where to drop the file in by hand. An agent's ingest asks the legal chain alone (never a fetcher the config marks unauthorised); `legalOnly: false` is refused unless a person allowed agents more. Input is a DOI or `arxiv:<id>`.

legalOnly.description: The legal open-access chain only (the default) — never a fetcher the config marks unauthorised; false is refused unless a person allowed agents more

tools.name: archive
tools.description: Internet Archive — for the out-of-print scholarly books the open-access pipeline cannot reach. `query` searches, `id` shows one item's files, and `id` with `import: true` fetches it. PUBLIC items only: a lending-only scan is reported and refused, because borrowing it on archive.org is the only legitimate way to read it.

tools.name: candidates
tools.description: The NEW SOURCES found for the research goals by the deterministic search (no model): each goal's saved queries on OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC, arXiv (and CORE with a key), the works citing its sources and its sources' authors' newer works, each read from the day it was last read, deduplicated by DOI against the corpus and the acquisition list. Default: the `new` (unseen) candidates of every goal, or of `goal`; `state` = new, seen, queued or dismissed. Filter them yourself: `mark` (candidate ids) with `as` = seen, queued or dismissed records your decision; `sweep: true` (with `goal`) reads the goal's watches now (`dryRun: true` stores nothing). Queue what is worth acquiring with the `queue` tool or `ingest_doi`.

tools.name: collection
tools.description: The library's SOURCE COLLECTIONS — the user's Calibre library (`name`: calibre, the default) and archive.org (archive-org; use the `archive` tool for it). `action`: `list` (the collections and whether the server reaches them) · `search` (`query`, `limit`; `unlinked: true` = the entries no source links) · `import` (`id` into the corpus; `citekey`, `format`, `convert: false` = the record only) · `link` (`citekey` to entry `id`) · `push` (`citekey`'s stored original as a new entry; `replace: true` swaps the linked entry's file) · `update` (`citekey`'s entry from its record; without `citekey`, every linked entry — a dry run unless `apply: true`) · `set` (`id`, `fields` as `name:value`) · `audit` · `gaps` (sources with a fetched file not in Calibre) · `sync` (push the gaps; a dry run unless `apply: true`). Writes need the Calibre GUI closed.

tools.name: research_state
tools.description: The research state: every open item and who acts next. Waiting for the owner, grouped by what to do (decide, download in the browser, borrow, buy or borrow, add an identifier, look at a stuck provider, resume a paused run, do a task); what the agents will handle, grouped by when (now, today, later). Filters: `who` (owner | agents), `goal` (a goal's slug), `kind` (decision | acquisition | task | run). Use to see what is yours to do and what to leave to the person.

tools.name: acquire_why
tools.description: Why one acquisition-list item is where it is: its verdict (who acts and why) and its kept attempts, with what each provider answered. `id`: the item's id (`#123` in `queue acquire`).
